rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As poets’ fame and poetry faded after their time, the Prophet’s eloquence would briefly stir attention and then its rise would end.
rows.anchor: similarly, for some time this person’s (the Prophet’s) eloquence and articulacy will cause a stir; but soon this rise will have a fall.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the opponents are waiting for a misfortune to end the Prophet’s mission, he is told to wait too and see whether their wish or God’s threat comes to pass.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) should tell them to wait as well and that he too is waiting to see whether their foolish desire is fulfilled

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-munūn means time; the idioms dāra ʿalayhim al-munūn and rayb al-munūn refer to time’s misfortunes and mishaps.
rows.anchor: which means “he became prey to the misfortunes of time.” The expression

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an refutes the charge that the Prophet is a poet at length in Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ, where it gives criteria for judging whether the Qur’an and its bearer can be compared with poetry and poets.
rows.anchor: In that sūrah, the Qur’ ān has presented a certain criteria on the basis

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They either use reason to deny the Prophet’s mission and call him a soothsayer, poet, or madman, or rebel from haughtiness; the author says the first is unlikely and arrogance drives the charge.
rows.anchor: it is their haughtiness which is inducing them to say such things; their intellect has no role in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opponents allege that the Prophet fabricated the Qur’an and falsely claimed that God revealed it through an angel to deceive people.
rows.anchor: their opinion is that though the Prophet (sws) has fabricated this Book yet to deceive the masses it is claimed that it is from God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb used for fabricating means to falsely accuse someone.
rows.anchor: The verb h means to falsely accuse someone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The assertion that they do not believe exposes the charge as contrary to their conscience: they know the Prophet did not author the Book.
rows.anchor: this allegation of theirs is also against the call of their conscience. They are fully certain that the Prophet (sws) has not authored

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They know the Prophet could not have produced the Qur’an, yet refuse faith and make a fabricated-authorship charge to conceal their wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: they know full well that such a discourse can neither be produced by him nor by anyone else; however, they do not want to profess faith in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb in this passage expresses intention, a usage for which the author says he has given earlier examples in the commentary.
rows.anchor: In my opinion, the verb here expresses intention. Several examples of such usage have been indicated earlier on in this exegesis.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In answer to the fabrication charge, the opponents are challenged to produce comparable discourse, either from earlier poets and orators or by composing it themselves.
rows.anchor: they should produce such a discourse from the poets and orators of the past or even sit together themselves and produce something in response.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge suited the Quraysh’s original setting and remains unanswered: neither past literary and religious works nor later efforts have produced a response.
rows.anchor: this challenge stands even today. The rejecters of the Qur’ ān have neither been able to produce something like it from their literary and religious treasures of the past

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For non-Arabs the challenge is indirect; its scope is the Qur’an’s overall quality as guidance, since literary excellence in one skill cannot establish prophethood.
rows.anchor: this challenge of the Qur’ ān is not just from one aspect; it is an over all challenge as a scripture of guidance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The questions challenge those who deny the Hereafter to say whether they were created without a creator, created themselves, or created the heavens and earth.
rows.anchor: they should speak up and say whether they have been created without a creator or whether they are their own creators. They should, moreover, tell whether they have created the heavens and the earth?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The One able to create people initially can recreate them; since He created and sustains them, He will ask whether they fulfilled their purpose.
rows.anchor: when they are not their own creators and in fact someone else has created them who has also arranged for their livelihood and sustenance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People did not create the heavens, earth, or their blessings, so they owe their Creator gratitude and will answer for their conduct in the world He made for them.
rows.anchor: the heavens and the earth and the blessings found in them and between them they benefit from. So, do they not owe any obligation to Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because they did not create the world, they should not feel safe from its Creator, who can shake the earth or destroy them with storms, hail, or stones.
rows.anchor: He can shake and jolt the earth whenever He wants to and they will be totally ravaged. Also, whenever He wants, He can unleash on them tempestuous winds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Rather, they are not certain” reveals that they evade the implications of premises they accept because they lack conviction that they personally deserve punishment if they do not reform.
rows.anchor: they do accept and acknowledge all the principal factors which necessitate the advent of the Hereafter and the reward and punishment that will take place on that Day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object of “they are not certain” is omitted because context makes clear that it is either the Hereafter or punishment.
rows.anchor: is suppressed because of clear contextual indications.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh did not flatly deny the Hereafter; they treated it as an improbable folk tale, too distant to worry about, or something their deities’ intercession would avert.
rows.anchor: they regarded it to be improbable. They believed that the Day of Judgment and the reward and punishment which would take place on that Day was a mere folk tale

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They also dismissed threatened punishment in this life, treating their greater affluence than the Prophet and his companions as proof that their own beliefs and deeds were sound.
rows.anchor: They regarded their existing status of affluence to be an argument in support of the veracity of their beliefs and deeds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says many Muslims likewise profess the Hereafter but lack conviction in it, as their lives show, and have been misled by notions like those of Arabia’s idolaters.
rows.anchor: These Muslims do not reject the Hereafter and its reward and punishment; however, their lives bear witness to the fact that they do not have conviction in these things.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since they neither created the heavens and earth nor possess God’s treasuries or control their distribution, the affluent cannot assume immunity or permanent luxury; God can take wealth and give it to others.
rows.anchor: they also cannot claim that the Almighty has given His treasures of sustenance and favours in their custody or has deputed them on their distribution

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh and affluent people of earlier nations treated wealth as an entitlement and ignored prophetic warnings, though God can strip or transfer it instantly.
rows.anchor: they regarded their affluence to be their birthright and for this reason they showed indifference to the warnings of the Prophet (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse refutes elites who argued that a divine messenger or bearer of true religion should have been a wealthy Makkan or Ṭāʾif notable rather than Muḥammad, the poor, or slaves.
rows.anchor: then He would have selected some rich person of Makkah or Ṭā’if and not a poor and destitute person like Muḥammad (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next question challenges their assumption that they will keep worldly luxuries and remain superior in the Hereafter by asking whether they can overhear God’s decisions.
rows.anchor: The implied meaning of this verse is:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical questions ask whether they can overhear divine decisions, have scripture promising their wishes, hold a written acquittal, or cite a divine informant; if so, they must prove it.
rows.anchor: Has the Almighty given them His written acquittal so that they can indulge in whatever mischief they want to and He will neither hold them accountable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author reads this question in light of Sūrah al-Qalam, which develops the claims of a scripture promising desires or binding divine oaths securing them.
rows.anchor: S ūrah al-Qalam comprehensively deals with this subject. I have interpreted this verse in the light of Sūrah al-Qalam.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabic is elliptical; he reconstructs the sense as asking whether they have a ladder resting against the sky by which they climb to eavesdrop.
rows.anchor: there are a few instances of ellipses. If they are unveiled the whole discourse would be something to the effect

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People need revelation for guidance: each person would need evidence of access to it, and since not everyone can claim that access, people must trust those who possess it.
rows.anchor: man, for his guidance, needs divine revelation. Now either every person should provide evidence that he has the means to receive divine revelation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If their confidence rests on intercessors protecting them in both worlds, their claim is exposed as baseless: they assign daughters to God while preferring sons and hating daughters, contrary to human nature.
rows.anchor: they contend daughters for God whereas they themselves like sons and hate daughters.
